questions.question: What is the difference between a unit test and an integration test in Spring Boot?
questions.title: Unit vs Integration Test
questions.direct_answer: A **unit test** checks a small unit of behavior in isolation and normally does not start Spring; collaborators may be real lightweight objects, fakes, or mocks. An **integration test** checks that multiple parts work together. In a Spring Boot project that may mean a test slice, a full ApplicationContext, a real database, or an HTTP boundary—Spring startup is common, not part of the definition.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate understands the testing pyramid and knows when each test type is appropriate in a Spring Boot project.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for service tests and calling them unit tests, or thinking unit tests always require Spring context.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that the useful distinction is the behavior boundary: a unit test isolates a small unit, while an integration test checks collaboration across a real boundary

sections.title: Two Different Testing Approaches
sections.content:
A **unit test** checks a small unit of behavior in isolation. It often supplies collaborators as fakes or Mockito mocks and normally does not start Spring. An **integration test** checks that multiple parts work together across a real boundary. In a Spring Boot project that boundary might be MVC configuration, persistence, the full ApplicationContext, a database, or an HTTP server.

Starting Spring is common in integration tests, but it is not the definition. Likewise, mocks are a technique rather than a requirement for every unit test. Choose the smallest boundary that can reveal the failure you care about, and keep a smaller test only when its doubles still model the contract accurately.

sections.title: Unit vs Integration at a Glance
sections.content:
emerald|Unit test|~Small isolated behavior|normally no Spring context|real lightweight objects or doubles|fast feedback
blue|Integration test|~Parts work together|slice or broad context|database or HTTP may be real|cost depends on boundary
amber|Test portfolio|~Shape follows risk|many focused checks|enough boundary tests|no universal percentages
rose|Common trap|~Label by annotation|Spring startup is not the definition|mocks are not the definition|name the boundary

sections.title: Unit Test vs Integration Test
sections.content:
| Aspect | Unit Test | Integration Test |
|---|---|---|
| Boundary | Small behavior in isolation | Collaboration across a real boundary |
| Spring context | Normally absent | Optional; often a slice or broader context |
| Collaborators | Lightweight real objects, fakes, or mocks | More real infrastructure and configuration |
| Cost | Usually lower | Usually higher and environment-dependent |
| Failure signal | Local logic or contract with a double | Wiring, mapping, persistence, protocol, or configuration |

sections.title: Unit Test — Isolated With Mocks
Integration Test — Real Wiring
When to Use Each Test Type
sections.content: Use a **unit test** for business rules, validators, mappers, and other behavior that can be proved with a small object graph. Use an **integration test** when the requirement depends on Spring wiring, MVC mapping, serialization, transaction behavior, a database dialect, or another real boundary. There is no correct universal percentage or timing ratio. Let risk, feedback time, and the kinds of defects found by the suite determine the mix.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Unit test** — checks a small behavior in isolation and normally needs no Spring context.
- **Integration test** — verifies collaboration across a real boundary; it may use a slice, a broad context, a database, or HTTP.
- **MockitoExtension** — convenient for Mockito-created doubles, but not required for every unit test.
- **@SpringBootTest** — one option for broad Boot integration, not the definition of every integration test.
- **Test portfolio** — use many fast checks and enough realistic boundary tests for the system's risks; fixed percentages are not a rule.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A unit test checks a small unit of behavior in isolation and normally does not start Spring. Its collaborators may be lightweight real objects, fakes, or mocks. An integration test checks that parts work together across a real boundary. In Spring Boot that could be a web slice, a repository with a database, a broad ApplicationContext, or a running HTTP server. For example, I would unit-test an order discount with a controlled repository result, then use @DataJpaTest to prove that the real order mapping and query work with the configured test database. Integration tests usually cost more because they create more infrastructure or perform I/O, but there is no fixed timing or correct percentage. I choose the smallest boundary that can prove the requirement, then add realistic integration coverage where mocks cannot expose wiring, mapping, persistence, or protocol errors.

questions.question: Why are unit tests faster than integration tests in a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Why Unit Tests Are Faster
questions.direct_answer: Unit tests are usually faster because they create only the object graph needed for one behavior and avoid broad framework startup and external I/O. Integration tests may build an ApplicationContext, migrate a database, start a server, or contact containers. There is no universal timing: measure the suite, reuse cached contexts, and keep each test at the smallest boundary that proves the requirement.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of what actually makes tests slow—context startup, I/O, network—not just code complexity.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking unit tests are faster simply because they test less code or have fewer assertions.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name the actual costs—context creation, migrations, containers, server startup, and I/O—and say that the suite should be measured rather than assigned a universal timing

sections.title: What Makes Tests Slow
sections.content:
Unit tests are usually faster because they create only the small object graph needed for the behavior and avoid broad framework startup and external I/O. An integration test may create an ApplicationContext, scan and initialize beans, run database migrations, start containers or a server, and perform network or database operations.

Those costs vary greatly by application, machine, cache reuse, and test design. A cached slice can be quick, while a badly designed unit test can still be slow. Measure the suite and its setup phases instead of teaching fixed millisecond or second ranges.

sections.title: Where the Time Goes
sections.content:
rose|Framework setup|~Possible integration cost|create context|initialize beans and pools|run migrations
amber|I/O|~Environment-dependent|database calls|network and containers|serialization and server path
emerald|Focused unit path|~Small object graph|direct method calls|controlled collaborators|normally no framework startup
blue|Improve feedback|~Measure first|reuse compatible contexts|avoid repeated setup|parallelize only when safe

sections.title: Speed Comparison Example
When Speed Matters
sections.content:
Fast feedback matters during local development and in CI, but no test category has one fixed duration. Measure discovery, context creation, database migration, container startup, network work, and the test body separately. Spring's context cache can reduce repeated setup when cache keys match in the same process.

Keep simple deterministic rules at a small boundary. Use integration tests where real mappings, queries, transactions, serialization, messaging, or configuration are the behavior being proved. Improve a slow suite by measuring its bottleneck, removing accidental context variation, sharing safe setup, and running independent groups in parallel where the tools and resources allow it.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Counting assertions instead of setup**: Context creation, migrations, containers, and I/O often dominate the cost.
- **Using a universal threshold**: Compare with the suite's baseline and inspect setup separately from test execution.
- **Using @DirtiesContext as database cleanup**: It evicts a Spring context. Use a test transaction when its boundary fits, or clean database state explicitly; Testcontainers does not by itself reset data between every test.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Smaller setup** — a unit test normally creates only the objects needed for one behavior.
- **Integration costs vary** — context startup, migrations, containers, server startup, and I/O depend on the environment.
- **Cache reuse matters** — compatible Spring tests can reuse a context in the same process.
- **Measure the suite** — use test reports and context-cache logging instead of fixed ratios or thresholds.
- **Optimize the boundary** — keep the realistic boundary needed to catch the defect; remove setup that does not contribute.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: Unit tests are usually faster because they create a small object graph and avoid broad framework startup and external I/O. An integration test may create a Spring context, initialize pools, run migrations, start a container or server, and call a database or network service. The actual time depends on the application, machine, cache reuse, and test boundary, so I would not quote a universal threshold. I measure the test report and context-cache behavior, then keep each test at the smallest boundary that can still reveal the wiring, persistence, or protocol defect I need it to catch.

questions.question: In a Spring Boot project, what does a typical unit test look like compared to an integration test?
questions.title: Unit vs Integration Test Structure
questions.direct_answer: A typical unit test constructs the subject directly and may use MockitoExtension with @Mock for controlled collaborators. An integration test selects the real boundary it needs: for example @WebMvcTest for MVC, @DataJpaTest for JPA, or @SpringBootTest for broader Boot wiring. The annotations suggest the setup, but the exercised boundary determines the test type.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate can write or recognize both test types and knows the annotation differences from memory.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest on a service unit test, wasting context startup time and calling it a unit test.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show both test structures from memory with correct imports and explain why each annotation is chosen for its purpose—demonstrate you've written both types in real projects.

sections.title: Structural Differences in Test Classes
sections.content:
A typical **unit test** constructs the subject directly and controls its collaborators. MockitoExtension, @Mock, and @InjectMocks are convenient options, not requirements. Assertions should focus on observable behavior; verifying every internal call can make a test brittle.

An **integration test** selects the boundary it needs. @WebMvcTest can exercise MVC configuration with MockMvc, @DataJpaTest can exercise mappings and queries, and @SpringBootTest can create broader Boot wiring. It may still replace a remote collaborator with a mock. Read the setup together with the behavior and infrastructure actually exercised instead of classifying solely by annotation.

sections.title: Read the Annotations to Tell Them Apart
sections.content:
emerald|Unit shape|~Mockito wiring|@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension)|@Mock plus @InjectMocks|verify() on mocks
blue|Integration shape|~Spring wiring|@SpringBootTest|@Autowired real beans|MockMvc or TestRestTemplate
amber|Imports tell|~Quick recognition|Mockito plus JUnit is unit|Spring Test is integration|read it in review
rose|Trap|~@SpringBootTest on a service|4s startup for logic|called integration|prefer Mockito here

sections.title: Unit Test vs Integration Test Structure
sections.content:
| Element | Unit Test | Integration Test |
|---|---|---|
| Boundary | Small behavior in isolation | Real collaboration or infrastructure |
| Common setup | Constructor plus fakes or mocks | Slice, context, database, server, or container |
| Spring context | Normally absent | Present when Spring-managed behavior is tested |
| Doubles | Optional | May still isolate an out-of-scope remote dependency |
| Assertions | Observable rule or result | Mapping, wiring, persistence, protocol, or workflow |

sections.title: Unit Test Structure — Mockito Only
Integration Test Structure — Real Context
When Each Structure Fits
sections.content: Use direct construction for a rule that does not require Spring-managed behavior. Use MockMvc when the MVC pipeline is the boundary, a persistence slice when mappings or queries are the boundary, and a real server only when the network/server path matters. @SpringBootTest without a port mode does not itself start a real server, and @DataJpaTest may use an embedded replacement unless configured otherwise.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **@ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class)** — initializes supported Mockito annotations for a JUnit Jupiter test; direct Mockito calls or manual construction are alternatives.
- **@Mock** — creates a Mockito test double that is not automatically a Spring bean.
- **@InjectMocks** — asks Mockito to construct or populate the subject from available mocks; ambiguous or missing dependencies still need explicit setup.
- **@SpringBootTest** — creates a Boot ApplicationContext shaped by the test configuration; it is broader, not automatically production-identical.
- **@Autowired** — injects a bean from that context, which can itself be a test override such as @MockitoBean.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A typical unit test constructs one subject and supplies controlled collaborators; MockitoExtension with @Mock is a common convenience. An integration test names the real boundary: WebMvcTest with MockMvc for MVC behavior, DataJpaTest for JPA behavior, or SpringBootTest for broader Boot wiring. It may use @Autowired for context beans and can still mock an out-of-scope remote dependency. I identify the test by what it truly exercises, not just by seeing Mock, Autowired, or SpringBootTest in the file.

questions.question: What is the testing pyramid and how does it apply to Spring Boot applications?
questions.title: Testing Pyramid in Spring Boot
questions.direct_answer: The **testing pyramid** is a heuristic: keep broad feedback cheap with many focused tests, add fewer boundary and integration tests, and use the most expensive end-to-end checks selectively. It does not prescribe fixed ratios or require every service test to mock a repository. Shape the mix around risk, architecture, execution cost, and the failures each level can detect.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has a structured view of testing strategy, not just knowledge of individual annotations.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing integration tests for everything or ignoring unit tests entirely, creating an inverted pyramid that makes the test suite unbearably slow.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Map each Spring testing annotation to its pyramid layer and explain the trade-off: more tests at the base means faster feedback loops, but you need some higher-layer tests to catch real-world integration bugs.

sections.title: The Testing Pyramid Strategy
sections.content:
The **testing pyramid** is a heuristic: keep a broad base of small, focused tests and use progressively fewer tests as the exercised boundary becomes broader, slower, or harder to isolate. It is not a required percentage chart.

In Spring Boot, the base may contain plain unit tests, the middle may contain MVC and persistence slices or other integration tests, and the top may contain a smaller set of real-server or system tests. The right shape depends on architecture and risk. The goal is fast local diagnosis plus enough realistic coverage to catch mapping, wiring, persistence, protocol, and deployment defects.

sections.title: The Three Layers Mapped to Spring
sections.content:
emerald|Base|~Focused checks|small behavior boundary|plain unit tests|fast diagnosis
blue|Middle|~Integration boundaries|@WebMvcTest or @DataJpaTest|database and messaging tests|real contracts
rose|Top|~Broad workflows|real server or system|critical journeys|fewer because cost and diagnosis grow
amber|Adapt the shape|~No fixed percentages|architecture matters|measure feedback|cover real risks

sections.title: Pyramid Layers in Spring Boot
Applying the Pyramid to Spring Boot Projects
sections.content: Start with focused tests for business rules and edge cases. Add @WebMvcTest where the MVC contract matters and @DataJpaTest where mappings or queries matter. Add broader @SpringBootTest or real-server tests for workflows whose risk lies in cross-layer configuration. Do not force a 70/20/10 split or a universal suite-duration target; measure feedback time and inspect which escaped defects the current mix misses.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating the pyramid as fixed ratios**: It is a feedback-and-cost heuristic; system risk and architecture decide the useful mix.
- **Assuming broader always means better**: A large context can hide the source of failure and still replace important external boundaries.
- **Assuming smaller always means sufficient**: Unit tests cannot prove mappings, transactions, serialization, or real infrastructure behavior.
- **Quoting fixed speedups**: Slice and full-context cost depends on configuration, cache reuse, hardware, and external resources.
- **Testing implementation details**: Prefer observable behavior over incidental internal call order unless that interaction is the contract.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Pyramid shape** — many focused checks and progressively fewer broad, costly workflows.
- **No fixed ratios** — architecture, risk, and feedback needs determine the mix.
- **Base** — isolated rules and edge cases with small object graphs.
- **Middle** — MVC, persistence, messaging, and other real integration boundaries.
- **Top** — critical workflows across a running system or several services.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: The testing pyramid is a heuristic for balancing feedback and realism. The broad base contains focused tests that isolate rules and fail clearly. The middle checks real boundaries such as MVC mapping, persistence, or messaging. The top covers a smaller number of critical workflows through a running system. In Spring Boot, that can map to plain JUnit tests, test slices, and broader SpringBootTest or system tests. The exact percentages and timings are not rules; I shape the suite around architecture, risk, feedback speed, and the defects that smaller tests cannot catch.

questions.question: Should you test your Spring service layer with unit tests or integration tests? Why?
questions.title: Testing the Service Layer
questions.direct_answer: Use unit tests for service rules that can be proved with a small object graph, and integration tests for behavior that depends on Spring proxies, transactions, persistence mappings, queries, configuration, or other real boundaries. A service often needs both. Mocks are useful at a boundary, but a fake or real lightweight collaborator can be clearer; speed differences must be measured rather than assumed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical judgment about which test type belongs at which layer of a Spring Boot application.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for every service test, making the suite very slow without gaining meaningful coverage.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that one service can need focused rule tests plus integration tests for proxies, transactions, persistence, or messaging boundaries

sections.title: Service Layer Testing Strategy
sections.content:
A service often deserves **both** focused and integration coverage. Use a unit test for validation, calculations, branching, and orchestration rules that can be proved with a small object graph. Collaborators may be mocks, fakes, or lightweight real objects.

Use integration tests when the service's behavior depends on Spring proxies, transaction boundaries, persistence mappings and queries, events, security, caching, or another real infrastructure contract. The mix is driven by risk; there is no universal service-layer percentage or rule that every repository must be mocked.

sections.title: Match the Layer to the Test
sections.content:
emerald|Service rules|~Focused unit test|validation and calculations|small object graph|mock, fake, or real collaborator
blue|Persistence behavior|~Integration test|mapping and query|transaction boundary|database chosen for confidence
amber|Spring-managed behavior|~Proxy-dependent|@Transactional|security or caching|events and configuration
rose|Cross-layer workflow|~Broader integration|several real components|server only if required|critical path

sections.title: Unit Testing a Service with Mocked Repository
When to Use Each Test Type
sections.content:
Use **unit tests** for service layer methods that transform data, validate input, calculate results, or orchestrate repository calls—anything that's pure logic. Example: testing that a pricing service applies the correct discount based on customer tier.

Use **integration tests** when you need to verify that a custom JPQL query returns the right rows, that @Transactional rollback works correctly, or that multiple services interact properly through Spring's dependency injection. Example: testing that an order creation flow correctly updates inventory, creates audit logs, and commits the transaction atomically. Reserve @SpringBootTest for **end-to-end scenarios** like "POST /orders should return 201 and persist to database."

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @SpringBootTest for local calculations**: A broad context can hide the simple behavior under test.
- **Mocking the persistence contract everywhere**: A mock cannot prove query semantics, mapping, constraints, or transaction behavior.
- **Assuming annotations work in a unit test**: Calling a service created with `new` does not apply proxy-based @Transactional, security, or caching behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Focused rules** — unit-test calculations, validation, branching, and orchestration with a small object graph.
- **Real boundaries** — integration-test persistence, transactions, messaging, security, caching, or proxy behavior when they matter.
- **Mocks are optional** — use a mock, fake, or lightweight real collaborator according to the contract.
- **MockitoExtension** — convenient for Mockito annotations, not the only valid unit-test setup.
- **@SpringBootTest** — use only when the behavior needs broad Boot wiring; a slice may be a better integration boundary.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: I normally give a service focused unit tests for its validation, calculations, branching, and orchestration rules. I construct a small object graph and use a mock, fake, or real lightweight collaborator according to the contract. I also add integration coverage where the behavior depends on Spring proxies, @Transactional semantics, persistence mappings or queries, events, security, caching, or other infrastructure. That means a service can need both kinds of test. I choose the smallest boundary that proves each requirement and measure suite cost rather than assuming a fixed speed ratio.

questions.question: What is a test slice in Spring Boot and why is it useful?
questions.title: What Are Test Slices
questions.direct_answer: A **test slice** limits Spring Boot component scanning and auto-configuration to a supported technical area. For example, **@WebMvcTest** focuses on MVC types and **@DataJpaTest** focuses on JPA. Imports, security, properties, and bean overrides can still change the context, so a slice is a focused boundary rather than a promise of one exact layer or speed.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Spring Boot's built-in test infrastructure beyond @SpringBootTest and knowing when to use slices.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using @SpringBootTest for everything, not knowing slice annotations exist, and ending up with unnecessarily slow tests.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Name multiple slices—@WebMvcTest, @DataJpaTest, @JsonTest, @RestClientTest—and explain what each loads and when to use it.

sections.title: Test Slices for Focused Layer Testing
sections.content:
A Spring Boot **test slice** limits component scanning and auto-configuration to a particular technical area. **@WebMvcTest** focuses on Spring MVC controllers and supported web infrastructure. **@DataJpaTest** focuses on JPA and is transactional by default; by default it uses an embedded test database when one is available, but that can be changed. **@JsonTest** focuses on JSON serialization support.

A slice usually creates less infrastructure than @SpringBootTest, but it is not a promise of a fixed speed or an exact bean count. Imports, security configuration, custom test configuration, and bean overrides can change the context. Choose the slice because its boundary matches the behavior under test.

sections.title: Common Slices at a Glance
sections.content:
blue|@WebMvcTest|~MVC slice|controllers and MVC infrastructure|MockMvc support|provide missing collaborators
emerald|@DataJpaTest|~JPA slice|repositories and JPA setup|transactional by default|embedded database can be replaced
amber|@JsonTest|~JSON slice|supported JSON components|serialize and deserialize|focused configuration
rose|Why slices|~Match one boundary|less unrelated setup|clearer failures|contexts can still be customized

sections.title: Using @WebMvcTest to Test a Controller
When to Use Each Slice
sections.content: Use **@WebMvcTest** for request mapping, validation, HTTP status, serialization, controller advice, filters, and other supported MVC behavior while supplying collaborators outside the slice. Use **@DataJpaTest** for repositories, mappings, and queries; it is transactional by default, and its database replacement behavior is configurable. Use **@JsonTest** for supported JSON serialization components. Use **@RestClientTest** for a supported REST-client slice. Use **@SpringBootTest** when the requirement genuinely needs broader Boot wiring.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Treating a slice as one exact bean list**: Imports, properties, security, and test overrides can change the context.
- **Combining unrelated slice annotations**: Each slice selects its own bootstrap and auto-configuration. Choose one focused boundary or define a broader test deliberately.
- **Assuming every absent collaborator needs a mock**: Use @MockitoBean or older @MockBean for a controlled double, @Import for a small real component, or broader configuration when its behavior is required.
- **Promising a fixed speed**: A slice usually avoids unrelated setup, but measure the real suite.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Test slice** — limits scanning and auto-configuration to a supported technical area.
- **@WebMvcTest** — focuses on MVC controllers and supported web infrastructure.
- **@DataJpaTest** — focuses on JPA, is transactional by default, and can replace the database according to configuration.
- **@JsonTest** — focuses on supported JSON components and ObjectMapper configuration.
- **Missing collaborators** — supply them with current @MockitoBean, older Boot @MockBean, @Import, or a small test configuration as appropriate.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A test slice limits Spring Boot scanning and auto-configuration to a supported technical area. WebMvcTest focuses on MVC controllers and web infrastructure; DataJpaTest focuses on JPA and is transactional by default; JsonTest focuses on JSON support. The exact context can still change through imports, security setup, properties, and bean overrides. When a controller collaborator is outside the MVC slice, I can provide it with current @MockitoBean, older Boot @MockBean, or import a small real configuration. I choose a slice because the boundary matches the behavior and avoids unrelated setup, not because it guarantees a fixed startup time.

questions.question: What happens when you annotate a test with @SpringBootTest?
questions.title: What @SpringBootTest Does
questions.direct_answer: **@SpringBootTest** builds a Boot ApplicationContext from the selected configuration, applies the active profiles and properties, and creates the beans required by that context. It does not guarantee a production-identical environment or a connection to every external system; test configuration, mocks, disabled auto-configuration, and the chosen webEnvironment can all change what starts.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of what @SpringBootTest actually does under the hood and the cost it incurs.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming it starts every bean, database, server, and external connection, or that its environment is automatically identical to production.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention webEnvironment parameter options—MOCK, RANDOM_PORT, DEFINED_PORT, NONE—and context caching between tests.

sections.title: Full Application Context Startup
sections.content:
@SpringBootTest asks Spring Boot to create an ApplicationContext through **SpringApplication** using the selected Boot configuration. Eligible component scanning and auto-configuration run, and the test's profiles, properties, webEnvironment, imports, exclusions, and bean overrides shape the result.

It does not guarantee that every application bean or external connection starts, and the environment is not automatically identical to production. MOCK opens no server port; RANDOM_PORT and DEFINED_PORT do. Use it when broad Boot wiring is part of the behavior being checked, and use a smaller unit test or slice when that boundary is sufficient.

sections.title: What @SpringBootTest Sets in Motion
sections.content:
emerald|What it does|~Boots the full app|scans components|reads application.yml|auto-configures everything
blue|webEnvironment|~Controls the web layer|MOCK is default|RANDOM_PORT real server|NONE no web
amber|The cost|~Slow startup|10-30s for medium apps|context is cached|reuse if config matches
rose|Use it for|~True integration|cross-layer flows|critical happy paths|not isolated logic

sections.title: Using @SpringBootTest for an End-to-End Test
When to Use @SpringBootTest
sections.content: Use **@SpringBootTest** when you need to verify that multiple layers of your application work together correctly in a realistic scenario. Examples: testing that a REST endpoint correctly processes a request, calls the service, persists to the database, and returns the expected HTTP response. Testing that scheduled jobs execute with the correct transaction behavior. Testing that security filters and authentication work as configured. Testing that message listeners consume from a queue and update the database. Do NOT use @SpringBootTest for testing a single service method's business logic or a single controller's request mapping—those should use unit tests or slice tests instead. Reserve @SpringBootTest for **critical happy paths** and **complex cross-layer flows** that you can't validate any other way.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using @SpringBootTest for isolated logic**: A broad context adds setup without improving a test whose requirement is a local calculation.
- **Confusing MOCK with a server**: The default mode opens no HTTP port; use RANDOM_PORT or DEFINED_PORT for a client that makes real network calls.
- **Assuming production equivalence**: Test profiles, properties, doubles, exclusions, embedded infrastructure, and environment differences can all change behavior.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Boot context startup** — creates the context from selected Boot configuration and eligible auto-configuration.
- **Test-specific environment** — profiles, properties, mocks, imports, and exclusions can differ from production.
- **webEnvironment.MOCK** — default; creates a mock web context when applicable but no listening server.
- **RANDOM_PORT or DEFINED_PORT** — starts a server for real HTTP calls.
- **webEnvironment.NONE** — creates a non-web context.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: @SpringBootTest creates a Boot ApplicationContext through SpringApplication. It can discover the main Boot configuration and apply eligible component scanning and auto-configuration. The exact beans and resources still depend on the test's profiles, properties, web environment, imports, exclusions, and bean overrides, so it is not automatically the same as production. MOCK is the default and opens no server port; RANDOM_PORT and DEFINED_PORT start a server, while NONE creates a non-web context. Spring can reuse contexts with the same TestContext cache key in the same process. I use this annotation when broad Boot wiring is part of the requirement, not for isolated Java logic.

questions.question: Can a Spring Boot test be both a unit test and use Spring annotations at the same time?
questions.title: Mixing Unit and Spring Annotations
questions.direct_answer: A unit test can use annotations, including JUnit or Mockito annotations, without becoming an integration test. What matters is the boundary it exercises. Loading a Spring ApplicationContext to test real Spring wiring makes it an integration-style test; merely using a small Spring utility or annotation does not automatically do so. Prefer plain construction when framework behavior is not under test.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate has clear conceptual boundaries between test types and doesn't blur the lines.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Adding @SpringBootTest to tests that only test a service method, treating all tests as integration tests.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that @ExtendWith(MockitoExtension.class) is the correct choice for unit tests and doesn't involve Spring at all—it's pure JUnit 5 and Mockito.

sections.title: Clear Boundaries Between Test Types
sections.content:
A unit test is defined by the **small behavior boundary it isolates**, not by the absence of every framework class or annotation. JUnit and Mockito annotations are common in unit tests. Code may also call a small Spring utility without starting an ApplicationContext and still be tested as a unit.

When a test loads a Spring ApplicationContext to verify real bean discovery, injection, transactions, MVC mapping, or other framework wiring, it is integration-style. The important question is what real boundary the test exercises. If framework behavior is not part of the requirement, construct the subject directly and supply its collaborators.

sections.title: Where the Line Is Drawn
sections.content:
emerald|Unit test|~Small isolated behavior|normally no context|direct construction|real lightweight objects or doubles
rose|Integration-style|~Real framework boundary|ApplicationContext loaded|bean wiring or transactions|MVC or persistence behavior
amber|Mock choices|~Different scopes|@Mock is a local Mockito double|@MockitoBean overrides a context bean|older Boot uses @MockBean
blue|Decision|~What is under test?|local behavior|framework collaboration|name the boundary

sections.title: True Unit Test Without Spring
When to Use Each Approach
sections.content: Use MockitoExtension when Mockito annotations make a focused unit test clearer. It is optional; hand-written fakes or direct construction can work too. Load Spring test support when the requirement concerns bean wiring, transactions, MVC behavior, repository mappings, or another real Spring boundary. Merely importing a Spring type does not decide the category; loading and exercising framework-managed collaboration does.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Classifying by annotation name**: The actual boundary and behavior under test matter more than whether a helper annotation comes from Spring.
- **Loading @SpringBootTest for local logic**: If wiring is not under test, direct construction gives a clearer, smaller test.
- **Confusing mock scopes**: @Mock creates a local Mockito mock. @MockitoBean, or @MockBean on older Boot, supplies or replaces a bean in a Spring test context.

sections.title: Quick revision
sections.content:
- **Unit test definition** — checks a small behavior in isolation; mocks are optional.
- **MockitoExtension** — initializes Mockito annotations without loading Spring.
- **@Mock vs context override** — @Mock is local; @MockitoBean or older @MockBean participates in a Spring context.
- **@InjectMocks** — asks Mockito to construct and inject the subject; explicit construction is often clearer when setup is simple.
- **Classify by boundary** — an ApplicationContext test of real wiring is integration-style; merely using a Spring utility is not.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content: A unit test can use JUnit, Mockito, or even a small Spring utility; the category is determined by the boundary it exercises. If the test loads an ApplicationContext to verify real bean wiring, transactions, MVC mapping, or persistence behavior, it is integration-style. If it constructs one subject directly and controls its collaborators, it remains a unit test even when those classes use Spring annotations in production. MockitoExtension is a convenient way to initialize local mocks, but it is not required. The practical rule is to start Spring only when Spring-managed behavior is part of the requirement.
